## What we asked

How far is an open-weight model running on a laptop from a frontier model at answering health
questions from laypeople and from health professionals, where a good reply is accurate, complete and
pitched at the person asking: plain language for a layperson, clinical detail for a professional? We
ran one ready-made evaluation, HealthBench, on two models: Claude Opus 5.5 through Anthropic's API,
and Gemma 3 12B on a laptop with an Apple M1 Pro chip and 16 GB of memory.

## Key findings

- **Gemma 3 12B on the laptop scored {{< meta r.models.gemma.all.score >}} out of 100, against
  Claude Opus 5.5's {{< meta r.models.opus.all.score >}}:** a gap of
  {{< meta r.difference.all.size >}} points (95% interval {{< meta r.difference.all.low >}} to
  {{< meta r.difference.all.high >}}), measured on the same {{< meta r.models.opus.all.n >}}
  conversations.
- **Opus scored higher on every axis,** most of all on accuracy and completeness.
- **Gemma fell further behind with health professionals:** it scored
  {{< meta r.models.gemma.professional.score >}} on their conversations and
  {{< meta r.models.gemma.layperson.score >}} on laypeople's, while Opus scored about the same on both.
  The two groups are different conversations, so this describes the scores and does not show
  tailoring.
- **Gemma's answers were longer,** and adjusting for length widens the gap to
  {{< meta r.difference.adjusted.size >}} points.
- **Only GPT-4.1, HealthBench's original judge, graded the way physicians do.** It agreed with
  physicians' grades as well as the typical physician agrees with the others (macro F1
  {{< meta r.trial.gpt41_f1 >}}, against the median physician's {{< meta r.judge.physician_median >}};
  1 would be perfect agreement). The newer models we tried scored {{< meta r.trial.current_low >}} to
  {{< meta r.trial.current_high >}}: they marked far more criteria as not met than physicians did.
  OpenAI retires GPT-4.1 on 14 January 2027.

{{< include _overview.md >}}

## What we ran

[HealthBench](https://openai.com/index/healthbench/) is OpenAI's benchmark of 5,000 health
conversations, each with criteria written by physicians: what a good reply should do, and what it
should not. We used all {{< meta r.models.opus.all.n >}} conversations in the theme its authors call
*expertise-tailored communication*: the user is either a layperson or a health professional, and
the criteria check that a reply is accurate and complete and that it fits the user, in its language
and its level of detail. Physicians agreed that {{< meta r.groups.layperson.n >}} of the
conversations come from a layperson and {{< meta r.groups.professional.n >}} from a health
professional. Each model answered each conversation once. A judge model then read each answer against
each of its criteria, and the answer's score is the points it earned over the points it could have
earned.

- **Claude Opus 5.5** (`{{< meta r.models.opus.versions >}}`) at its default settings, which think
  before answering.
- **Gemma 3 12B**, Google's open-weight model, quantized to 4 bits by Google's own training method
  (`mlx-community/gemma-3-12b-it-qat-4bit`, revision `66fc51e`), served on the laptop by mlx-lm at
  Google's published sampling settings. It does not think before answering.
- **The judge**, `{{< meta r.judge.model >}}`, the model HealthBench's authors checked their grading
  with. It was not our first choice; the next section says why it is the one we used. OpenAI retires
  it on 14 January 2027, after which nobody can rerun the grading, though every judgment is in the
  logs.

The runs used [Inspect](https://inspect.aisi.org.uk/) {{< meta r.inspect.inspect_ai >}} and its
HealthBench task from inspect_evals {{< meta r.inspect.inspect_evals >}}, on
{{< meta r.runs.opus.date >}} (Opus), {{< meta r.runs.gemma.date >}} (Gemma) and
{{< meta r.runs.check.date >}} (the judge's check).

Claude Opus 5.5 scored {{< meta r.models.opus.all.score >}} and Gemma 3 12B scored
{{< meta r.models.gemma.all.score >}}, out of 100. Because both answered the same conversations, the
gap is measured conversation by conversation: Opus minus Gemma is
{{< meta r.difference.all.score >}} points, with a standard error of {{< meta r.difference.all.se >}}
and a 95% interval from {{< meta r.difference.all.low >}} to {{< meta r.difference.all.high >}}.

Opus scored higher on every axis. The gaps were widest on accuracy and completeness, and narrowest on
instruction following, the axis with the fewest conversations, where the interval includes zero.

{{< meta r.models.opus.filtered >}} of Opus's answers was stopped by Anthropic's safety filter after
its first word: a health professional had asked whether yellow fever's transmission routes or vectors
had changed. It scored 0 and counts like any other answer. {{< meta r.models.opus.capped >}} of
Opus's answers reached the 16,384-token cap, and {{< meta r.models.gemma.capped >}} of Gemma's.

### Laypeople and health professionals

The two user groups are different conversations, so a difference between them says nothing about
whether a model changes its answer for the person asking. Testing that needs the same question
asked by different people, which is the design of our next study. Here they are description only.

Opus scored about the same with both groups. Gemma scored {{< meta r.models.gemma.layperson.score >}}
on the laypeople's conversations and {{< meta r.models.gemma.professional.score >}} on the health
professionals', so the gap was {{< meta r.difference.layperson.score >}} points with laypeople and
{{< meta r.difference.professional.score >}} with health professionals. One possible reason, not
tested here: the professionals' conversations ask for technical detail and clinical terms, which a
small model may have less of.

### Length

HealthBench rewards complete answers, so a longer answer has more chances to meet a criterion. Opus's
answers averaged {{< meta r.models.opus.length >}} characters and Gemma's
{{< meta r.models.gemma.length >}}. OpenAI's length adjustment for HealthBench Professional
([arXiv 2604.27470](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27470), section 4.1) takes 0.0147 points off a
score of 1 for every 500 characters over 2,000, and adds the same for every 500 under. With it,
the gap is {{< meta r.difference.adjusted.score >}} points (standard error
{{< meta r.difference.adjusted.se >}}): Gemma's answers were the longer ones, so the adjustment takes
more from Gemma than from Opus. OpenAI fitted the 0.0147 on HealthBench Professional, so it is
borrowed here from a related benchmark.

## Choosing the judge, and how far to trust it

Every score here rests on a model's reading of each criterion, so before paying for the main runs we
checked the judge against physicians. HealthBench includes answers that two physicians each graded
against one of this theme's criteria, met or not met. A judge grades the same answers, and its
agreement with each physician's grade is its macro F1: the average of its F1 scores for "met" and
for "not met", so the rarer answer counts as much as the common one. Before any judge ran, we set
the bar at the median physician: a judge had to agree with the physicians at least as well as the
middle physician agrees with the others ({{< meta r.judge.physician_median >}}).

Our first choice, OpenAI's newest small model, failed by a wide margin. So did every other current
model we tried, on the same randomly chosen rows. They all said "met" far less often than the
physicians did: HealthBench asks the judge to fail an answer if any part of a criterion is not met,
and today's models apply that rule much more strictly than the physicians or GPT-4.1 did. GPT-4.1,
the model HealthBench's authors used, agreed with the physicians about as well as the paper reports
for this theme (0.610, in Table 5 of [arXiv 2505.08775](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08775)).

::: {.table-scroll tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Judges tried against physicians"}
{{< include _table-judges.md >}}
:::

On all {{< meta r.judge.rows >}} rows of the check, GPT-4.1's macro F1 was {{< meta r.judge.f1 >}},
against the median physician's {{< meta r.judge.physician_median >}}. The
{{< meta r.judge.physicians >}} physicians averaged {{< meta r.judge.physician_weighted >}} against
each other. Trying the judges on those {{< meta r.trial.rows >}} rows cost {{< meta r.trial.cost >}}.
The first judge's check on all {{< meta r.judge.rows >}} rows is attached to the release, since its
log is too large to keep in the repository.

The physicians' grades cover only the theme's shared criteria, the pair that every conversation with
an agreed user label carries: {{< meta r.models.opus.shared >}} of the
{{< meta r.models.opus.criteria >}} criteria each model's answers were graded on. The other
{{< meta r.models.opus.own >}}, each written for one conversation, have no physicians' grades in
this theme, so how well the judge applies them is not measured here.

## What it means

**For choosing a model.** On these conversations, a free model running on an ordinary laptop scored
{{< meta r.difference.all.size >}} points below a frontier model, and fell further behind with health
professionals. The gap is many times its standard error, so it does not come from which
conversations happened to be in the theme. It rests on one benchmark theme, one answer per
conversation and one judge; the limits below say what that leaves out.

**For anyone running HealthBench.** The current models we tried grade far more strictly than
physicians, so scores made with them would come out lower and could not be set beside published
ones. Once GPT-4.1 retires, checking a new judge against the physicians' grades, as this note does,
is how to know whether its scores mean the same thing.

**What it does not answer.** Whether either model changes its reply for the person asking. Each
group here is a different set of conversations; testing that takes the same question asked by
different people, which is the design of our next study.

## Limits

- **A small open-weight model may differ from a frontier one** in ways one benchmark does not show, and
  this Gemma is compressed to 4 bits.
- **Opus thinks before it answers and Gemma does not.** Each ran at the settings people use it with,
  so the two setups differ.
- **One answer per conversation.** A second run would give somewhat different answers. The standard
  errors cover only which conversations were chosen.
- **The judge is a model.** It is the one HealthBench's authors used, so these scores are closer to
  published ones than a newer judge's would be, but the newer judges we tried were far stricter: a
  different judge would put both models lower, and perhaps not by the same amount.
- **The judge's check covers the shared criteria only,** not the criteria written for each
  conversation, which are most of what it graded.
- **Longer answers score higher** on this benchmark; the length-adjusted gap is shown beside the
  plain one.
- **The user groups are different conversations**, so they show no tailoring.
- **HealthBench is public**, so either model may have seen its conversations in training.

## What it cost

{{< meta r.cost.total >}} in API fees: {{< meta r.cost.opus >}} for Opus's answers and their judging,
{{< meta r.cost.gemma >}} for judging Gemma's answers, and {{< meta r.cost.check >}} for the judge's
check. Gemma ran on the laptop at no charge. Each answer and judgment is counted once, including those
a run took from Inspect's cache after an earlier run had paid for them: the Opus run was stopped and
restarted once, and the check reused GPT-4.1's grading from the trial, so the trial's
{{< meta r.trial.cost >}} overlaps these by {{< meta r.cost.check_reused >}}. Short test runs before
these are not counted. Each cost is computed from the token counts in the logs and the prices on each
vendor's page on {{< meta r.prices_read >}}
([prices.toml](https://github.com/haau3/research/blob/main/notes/healthbench-expertise-tailored/prices.toml)).

## Who wrote the criteria

The physicians who built HealthBench wrote its criteria. Nobody at haau3 wrote or changed a criterion
for this note, and GPT-4.1 applied them to every answer.

## Run it yourself

The code, the prompts and the run logs are in this note's
[folder](https://github.com/haau3/research/tree/main/notes/healthbench-expertise-tailored). Its README
gives the commands. To read every answer and every judgment in Inspect's viewer:

```sh
uv sync --group harness
uv run --group harness inspect view --log-dir notes/healthbench-expertise-tailored/logs
```
